name: MoE mixed-precision expert bit allocation (expert-level bit-width, not one fixed precision)
bits: per-expert or per-expert-group bit widths. The published endpoints span 2.25-bit (MxMoE), ~2-bit (MoQE, AlphaQ, EAQuant W2A4) and 4-bit W8A8-style expert weights; AutoScheme generates mixed-bit recipes in minutes
activation_scheme: the interesting cases are genuinely low-precision: EAQuant evaluates W4A4 / W3A4 / W3A3 / W2A4; MxMoE reports 5-bit weight-activation quantization with mixed precision
kernels: mixed-precision GroupGEMM - MxMoE's key systems contribution is that it automatically generates GroupGEMM kernels that execute GEMMs of DIFFERENT precisions in parallel; without such a kernel, mixed precision is a memory win only and may lose throughput
per-expert static scales in a compressed-tensors checkpoint; llama.cpp's llama_tensor_get_type_impl special-cases 8-expert (Mixtral) models
quality_delta: The only figures in this cluster with a named model, benchmark and delta are from MxMoE (qlab2-arxiv-mxmoe): 2.4 lower Wikitext-2 perplexity than GPTQ at 2.25-bit, up to 3.4x speedup over full precision, and up to 29.4% speedup over uniform quantization at equivalent accuracy with 5-bit weight-activation quantization. Model architectures are not named in the abstract, so treat as paper-claim-grade. MoQE (qlab2-arxiv-moqe) reports an INT2-mixed DeepSeek-R1-sized MoE at 79.6% model-size reduction vs fp16 and 1.24x A100 speed-up with an optimized runtime, but gives no benchmark name.
notes: NOT A PROXY BUT A NEAR MISS, DECLARED 2026-10-04: expert-level bit allocation is not a ModelOpt recipe - the sources are seven independent arXiv papers (AlphaQ, EAQuant, MoEQuant, MoE, MXMoE, QuantMoEBench, VSRAQ). 'modelopt' is defensible only in that ModelOpt is the common production path for this, but a query for ModelOpt returns a literature record that has no ModelOpt source. The grouping axis (per-expert) is genuinely different from every other record here, which is the more useful distinction. GROUP SIZE LEFT NULL 2026-10-04: the bit allocation here is per-EXPERT or per-expert-group, i.e. the axis is the expert, not a contiguous run of weights in one tensor. Different experts carry different bit widths, so a single weight group size does not exist for the model. THE CENTRAL FINDING, and the reason this is a distinct record rather than a note on the gptq/awq records: generic PTQ applies ONE fixed precision to the whole MoE, and that is what breaks. QuantMoE-Bench (qlab2-arxiv-quantmoebench) states the mechanism precisely - MoE's sparse routing produces DIFFERENT activation patterns, because shared experts are accessed by ALL tokens while token-conditioned experts are selectively activated, so the two do not have the same quantization requirement, and consistently-activated shared experts potentially need HIGHER precision to hold model quality. MxMoE adds a second, independent axis: divergent expert activation FREQUENCIES create heterogeneous computational characteristics, so mixed-precision choice must be co-designed with hardware rather than chosen for accuracy alone. DIRECTION OF THE EXPERT BIT ALLOCATION - note this is not uniform, and the papers disagree about which experts to favour, which is worth flagging rather than smoothing over. AlphaQ (qlab2-arxiv-alphaq), which is calibration-free, allocates MORE bits to experts whose weight spectra are more heavy-tailed, on the theory that heavy-tailed means better-trained. Colla-Q instead balances activation entropy across experts so no single expert collapses. QuantMoE-Bench argues the structurally correct answer is more bits for shared/always-on experts. These are three different selection criteria; none is established as the default. WHY CALIBRATION IS THE HARD PART, and it is the practical blocker: MoEQuant (qlab2-arxiv-moequant) names two distinct failures. INTER-EXPERT IMBALANCE: uneven sample distribution across experts leaves infrequently-used experts with insufficient and biased calibration. INTRA-EXPERT IMBALANCE: MoE's aggregation mechanism makes different samples correlate differently with their assigned expert. AlphaQ's motivation is the deployment version of the same problem - frontier MoE models are trained on proprietary data, so any calibration set is an imperfect surrogate and misestimates expert utilization. This connects directly to the imatrix record: a llama.cpp imatrix built from a corpus that under-exercises rarely-routed experts inherits exactly this bias. ECONOMICS, and it explains the whole subfield: MoE deployment is memory-bound because ALL expert weights must be resident even though only k are used per token, so precision reduction buys residency while the FLOPs stayed flat. MoQE's framing is that 2-bit expert weights can still beat the dense model trained on the same dataset - robustness of expert layers to quantization is doing real work here.
